To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
tools evoke more activity in tool-selecting areas than visually similar non-tools and that this effect is independent of the tool's orientation.
tools evoke greater activity in areas that are selective to tools over non-tools and that these areas include sensorimotor areas.
Passively viewing real tools, as opposed to non-tools matched on their low-level visual features, evokes activity in brain areas implicated in tool understanding and sensorimotor control.
